defect.found: The tensor store uses 64-hex filenames that LOOK like content addresses and are not. Across 12 randomly sampled tensors, ZERO have a filename equal to the sha256 of their contents, and none match the sha256 of the payload after the header, of the scales, of the codes, of the bf16 source as f32, or of the bf16 source raw. The manifest records no sha256, hash or digest field for any tensor.
defect.why_it_matters: G105's verify says 'rebuild from recipe, compare digests'. There were no digests to compare. G096's verify assumes content-addressed inputs. A substituted or corrupted tensor would not have been detected by name.
defect.fixed_forward: This seal now records a real sha256 for all 755 tensor files and a rolling digest over them, so a future rebuild has an anchor to compare against. That does NOT make the existing artifact reproducible -- it makes it VERIFIABLE from here on.

content_addressing.implication: Filenames that look like content addresses are recorded in receipts and must not be renamed, even when they are not actually the sha256 of their contents. The schema string hawking.nos.nr_nx_artifact.v1 is sealed. Renaming it invalidates this receipt.

sealed_schemas.rule: Every schema string below is excluded from renaming.

SAFE.target: None of the sealed identifiers, crate names, receipt filenames, or hashed paths
SAFE.reason: A name that is only used in uncommitted local scratch, or a *new* identifier introduced going forward under the surviving four (HCLI, Odyssey, Noetic, Gravity), can be chosen freely. That is not a rename of anything already on disk. There is no safe retroactive rename of a catalogued name in this tree: vestigial is not reclaimable, components are live gates, surviving names are the vocabulary, and ambiguous patients/schema-kinds are already baked into receipts.

SAFE.target: Future code and receipts using surviving vocabulary for new work
